awd_titl_txt: AGS-PRF: Evaluating Past Trends and Future Trajectories of Reactive Nitrogen Emissions from Agriculture--Air Quality and Radiative Forcing Impacts
awd_abstract_narration:
This Postdoctoral Research Fellowship (PRF) research focuses on the trends and impacts of agricultural releases of reactive nitrogen to the atmosphere. A scheme will be developed to assess reactive nitrogen emissions that account for transport and chemistry including pollutant lifetime as well as cross-information from all observed reactive nitrogen species. While reactive nitrogen is necessary for plant growth, its use leads to emissions of reactive nitrogen species with implications for radiative forcing and air quality.

The objectives of the project are to: (1) Exploit satellite and surface observations of nitrous oxide (N2O), ammonia (NH3), and nitrogen oxides (NOx) to jointly constrain global reactive nitrogen (Nr) emissions from agriculture over the past decade (2015-2024); (2) Assess the drivers (e.g. meteorology, economics) which best explain the inferred emissions trends and determine where and why 2015-2024 emissions trends diverge from the agricultural emissions projected by various forecasts of Nr; and (3) Simulate the air quality (fine particulate matter and ozone) and the radiative impacts of future Nr emissions scenarios, assuming a variety of agricultural intervention strategies and their interactions with fuel decarbonization pathways.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Because plants require nutrients to produce crops, farmers add reactive nitrogen to soils to enhance agricultural productivity. However, some reactive nitrogen escapes into the atmosphere, where it degrades air quality and alters the Earth’s energy budget. As air quality regulations reduce emissions from fossil fuels, agricultural emissions are expected to increase in importance, yet scientific understanding of reactive nitrogen emissions remains limited. In this fellowship, I have used satellite and surface data to investigate reactive nitrogen emissions from agriculture and have connected with policymakers and stakeholders to share results. Fellowship outcomes will continue to be delivered over the next several years, as I left the program early (after 9.5 months) to begin a tenure-track academic job.

Intellectual merit: This work has led to one submitted first-author paper so far, where we show using satellite observations that ammonia emissions have been increasing recently (2013–24), driven largely by livestock growth and chemical fertilizer applied to agricultural soils. Ammonia is a reactive nitrogen species that degrades air quality. We find that increased radiative forcing has also observably increased ammonia emissions in recent years, offsetting policy interventions like fertilizer controls, and we project that further forcing increases will drive ammonia emission increases by the end of the century. This work involved a novel fusion of machine learning with traditional Bayesian data assimilation, where we first used established methods to quantify ammonia emissions using satellite observations before using machine learning to estimate the mechanistic drivers of emission change. The new method pioneered here is widely applicable across the emissions quantification field; data and code are freely shared both to ensure robustness and reproducibility as well as to accelerate further development and application of our machine learning data fusion methodology. Fellowship support further allowed me to release several new versions of my CHEEREIO open-source data assimilation software and support its application to a wide variety of emission quantification problems, led by research groups around the world. One promising new application is to quantifying emissions of volatile organic compounds, including isoprene, led by collaborators at the University of Minnesota.

Additional fellowship-supported work in prep (1) investigates the seasonal cycle of ammonia emissions, and (2) simultaneously quantifies emissions of ammonia, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide to both capture a more complete nitrogen cycle as well as to better control for gas-particle partitioning. I expect to submit manuscripts on these topics, acknowledging NSF support, in the coming years. Because of the shortened timeframe of the funded work, two originally proposed items remain in earlier stages of research. My proposed investigation of nitrous oxide, which is important for the Earth’s energy balance, has been delayed because of difficulty estimating nitrous oxide emissions within acceptable error bounds due to sparse observations. However, some experiments suggest promising paths forward, and my new lab will return to the nitrous oxide problem to build on the initial experiments funded by this project. I also proposed investigating the interactions between radiative impacts on reactive nitrogen emissions and possible novel emissions sources, like ammonia engines on ships and aircraft; radiative impacts were quantified in the submitted manuscript, supporting a more comprehensive assessment to be addressed in future work.

Broader impacts: Proposed broader impacts included (1) research-driven outcomes informing international efforts to reduce pollution from agriculture such that interventions maximize radiative and air quality benefits while also advancing global development and food security; and (2) mentoring interested researchers, especially undergraduates, in order to build a stronger scientific workforce. Regarding item 1, in my fellowship I emphasized presenting research in forums that included policymakers and the private sector (focusing on agriculture) as well as in scientific forums. I accompanied my fellowship mentor Drew Shindell to a UN Environmental Program meeting in Ispra, Italy, where I was able to present findings supported here to a wide variety of stakeholders including global policymakers; additional forums included non-academic food system conferences in Atlanta, GA and Raleigh, NC as well as international scientific conferences including the GEOS-Chem meeting in June 2026 and the upcoming American Meteorological Society meeting in January 2027. Research items will continue to support international assessments of reactive nitrogen, such as that of the CCAC/FAO. To all these audiences, I have emphasized that diagnosing the dominant sectoral drivers of reactive nitrogen emissions change, and the increasing radiative penalty on emissions, has important implications for emission mitigation and air quality control. Regarding item 2, follow-on work will involve a wide set of undergraduates at Oberlin College, where I am now on the tenure-track faculty. From a professional development perspective, my stated fellowship goals of expanding my inverse modeling methods to agriculture, establishing an independent research agenda, and securing a tenure-track academic position were all achieved.
